preamble: A shift of the alveolar sibilant [s] to the labiodental fricative [f] moves the place of articulation from the tongue tip to the lower lip and upper teeth while keeping a voiceless fricative. It is rare as a regular change. The clearest documented case is Ofo, an extinct Siouan language of the lower Mississippi, in which Siouan *s and *z regularly became f (often recorded as aspirated fh), while the closely related Biloxi and the northern Siouan languages kept the sibilant.
phoneticEffects: Labialization, Change of Place of Articulation, Desibilantization

examples.note: Holmer (1947) states the correspondence as a regular development: Siouan s, z > Ofo fh, f; the initial i- is a prothetic vowel.

examples.from: Biloxi si, Ponca si, Dakota siha' 'foot'
examples.note: The sibilant kept by Biloxi and the Dhegiha and Dakota languages corresponds to Ofo fh.
Voegelin (1938) counts nine Ofo f : Biloxi s and nine Ofo fh : Biloxi s correspondences in the Dorsey-Swanton dictionary.

sources: Holmer, Nils M. (1947). An Ofo Phonetic Law. International Journal of American Linguistics 13(1): 1-8. https://lx.berkeley.edu/sites/default/files/holmer_-_ofo_phonetic_law.pdf
Voegelin, C. F. (1938). Ofo-Biloxi Sound Correspondences. Proceedings of the Indiana Academy of Science 48. https://journals.indianapolis.iu.edu/index.php/ias/article/view/5199
